issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 03-2026: Propriety of a family court judge attending a dinner hosted by a law firm at an annual legal conference.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO. 3 - 2026
RE:
Propriety of a family court judge attending a dinner hosted by a law firm at an annual legal
conference.
FACTS
Every year the South Carolina Association for Justice (“SCAJ,” formerly known as the
South Carolina Trial Lawyers Association), has an annual conference in August at Hilton Head.
During the conference, some of the larger law firms host dinners. The firms generally will arrange
transportation to and from the restaurant and pay for dinner and drinks for their invited guest.
Guests will generally include the attorneys of the hosting firm, along with other attorneys that
practice in the same area of law or who have referred cases to the firm. In addition, certain
members of the General Assembly and/or Judiciary are invited to attend various dinners.  Usually,
the judges invited will be judges before which the lawyers of the host firm regularly appear.
Each year, there have been judges in attendance at certain dinners; however, some judges
have expressed concerns that allowing the law firm to pay for such dinner could be a problem for
the bench.  In addition, there has been a growing concern that even if it is appropriate to accept the
dinner, the judge must disclose the cost of the judge’s meal, drinks, and transportation on the
judge’s annual report.  The inquiring judge requests an opinion as to: 1) Whether a judge may
attend a dinner hosted by a law firm that employs lawyers who appear before the judge? 2) If the
judge can attend such dinner, must the judge disclosure the cost of the dinner on the judge’s annual
financial disclosure?

CONCLUSION
A family court judge may attend a dinner hosted by a law firm at an annual legal
convention.
OPINION
Canon 2 (A) of the Code of Judicial Conduct requires that a judge conduct himself at all times in
a manner that promotes public confidence in the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.
However, a judge should not become isolated from the society in which he lives. Commentary,
Canon 4 (A). In Opinion 32-1994, this Committee addressed this issue, stating: “[j]udges cannot
be expected to sever all ties with society, including attending social occasions.”
In various opinions we have found that a judge can host a party or reception. See, Opinion
No. 17-1995 (permitting a judge to give a reception to thank friends in the community for allowing
him to serve them as an elected official); Opinion 10-1997 (judge could host a reception for city
employees and elected officials to express his appreciation); Opinion 07-2003 (family court judge
could host a reception for attorneys in the judicial circuit in which the judge presides, in order to
allow local lawyers and court personnel to meet on a non-work-related basis); and Opinion 1-2016
(judge and attorney son permitted to host a party for all judges attending the State Bar convention).
In addition, Canon 4 addresses gifts to judges and does allow a judge to accept “ordinary social
hospitality,” Canon 4D(5)(c).
While these opinions focus on the judge as host, they all involve a judge being able to
partake in social occasions, including ones that involve attorneys. Furthermore, in Op. 1-2016,
one of the hosts was an attorney who presumably appeared before the judges who would attend
the party. Thus, we see no violation of the Canons by allowing a judge to attend a dinner hosted
by a law firm at the SCAJ convention, even if some of the attorney dinner guests will appear
before the judge.
2

As to whether the judge must disclose the cost of the dinner and transportation on t

he
judge’s annual report, we have no opinion. “The purpose of the Committee shall be to render
written advisory opinions to inquiring judges concerning the propriety of contemplated judicial
and nonjudicial conduct.” Rule 503, SCACR. The Commentary to Canon 4D(5)(a)-(d) states
that:
A gift to a judge, or to a member of the judge's family living in the judge's
household, that is excessive in value raises questions about the judge's impartiality
and the integrity of the judicial office and might require disqualification of the judge
where disqualification would not otherwise be required.

The only monetary limitation discussed in the Canons states that a judge can accept:
any other gift, bequest, favor or loan, only if:  the donor is not a party or other
person who has come or is likely to come or whose interests have come or are likely
to come before the judge;  and, if its value exceeds $150.00, the judge reports it in
the same manner as the judge reports compensation in Section 4H[.]

Canon 4D(5)(e). In other words, “ordinary social hospitality” is different than any other
“gift, bequest, favor or loan” and not necessarily subject to the $150 limit. Thus, the judge
must use his or her discretion in determining whether a gift of ordinary social hospitality
is excessive. We also note that in Ethics Advisory Opinion 16-03, which addressed the
propriety of giving gifts to a new judge, that Committee stated:
The dollar value of the gift is not, by itself, determinative of the ethical inquiry.
There is, for example, no per se rule that a gift worth less than $150 is permissible
or that a gift worth more than $150 is impermissible. The dollar value of a gift is
relevant only in relation to the totality of the circumstances, including the nature
and duration of the relationship, the norms and customs of the community, the
number of lawyers contributing to the gift, and the nature of their practices.
